paras: The mob attack on an Italian prisoner at Corning, New York, took place on September 9, 1888, when a crowd of several hundred people stoned and clubbed an Italian laborer whom officers had arrested after the fatal shooting of John King in a saloon. Whether the man survived is disputed: most reports said he was nearly killed, while a later New-York Tribune dispatch said he died in the lockup within minutes. New York papers drew attention to the case because of reports that the crowd had attacked the wrong man.

According to The Sun, three Italian laborers were drinking in John Nealy's saloon on West Market Street at about 5 o'clock on Sunday afternoon when King joined them at the bar. A woman the paper named as May Caven came in, and when she showed affection toward King a fight broke out in which one of the Italians fired an old-fashioned pistol and killed him.
King, aged 25, unmarried and born in Ireland, had lived in Corning six years and worked at the Corning Glass Works, as a head potmaker according to The Sun and as foreman according to a wire brief.

The three Italians fled across the river toward Knoxville, a village where, The Sun said, a gang of Italian laborers lived. Officers caught one man, who, the Tribune later said, protested his innocence and already had cuts on his face. When the officers reached the bridge with him, a large crowd met them with threats and shouts to throw him in the river.

The crowd grew "ungovernable" and attacked the prisoner with paving stones and clubs until he fell unconscious. The officers pushed through to a livery stable while he was still being struck and then took him by carriage to the jail. The Sun reported that his head was cut and one eye partly torn out, and that doctors were summoned. A second Italian was later arrested in Knoxville and brought to Corning, but rain kept the crowd from mobbing him.

At the jail the woman reportedly said both arrested men were in the fight but neither fired the shot, and police and a large crowd searched for a third man. By the night of September 10, the Tribune's correspondent reported a rumor that the man attacked by the mob was innocent and that the guilty man had been arrested. No report of an inquest, of arrests among the crowd, or of a trial for King's killing appears in the coverage.

The New-York Tribune ran its first dispatch on September 10 under the headline "The Wrong Man Suffers for a Murder Done in a Drunken Brawl," and its front-page news summary said the mob had beaten almost to death an Italian arrested "for murder which another had committed." The next day it followed with "Did the Mob Kill the Wrong Man!" and reported the prisoner's death. Neither Tribune story condemned the crowd as such; both turned on the prisoner's possible innocence.

The Sun's fuller account also faulted the saloon, calling it one of the worst places in town, run by a special policeman, where Sunday laws were ignored. A condensed-news brief printed in the Wilmington Evening Journal and the Waterbury Evening Democrat on September 10 and in the Monmouth Inquirer on September 13 named the shooter as "Roos" and said he was recaptured and nearly killed by a mob, with no hint of doubt about his guilt. The Cambria Freeman of Ebensburg, Pennsylvania, said on September 14 only that officers caught one of three Italians and that a mob nearly killed him.

Accounts differ on who the prisoner was: the wire brief identified him as Roos, the shooter, while the Tribune and The Sun reported the woman's statement that he had not fired the shot. On his fate, the brief, the Tribune's summary and the Cambria Freeman said he was nearly killed, The Sun said he was jailed and doctors called, and the Tribune's September 10 dispatch said he died at the lockup. The Sun also said the crowd was told he was dead as he was carried away, and no other paper confirms the Tribune's report of his death.

reader.title: Mob attack on an Italian prisoner at Corning, New York
bases: A crowd of several hundred stoned and clubbed a prisoner held by officers on suspicion of a fatal shooting, with calls to throw him in the river (A1, A3, A6).

A crowd of several hundred attacked a man arrested for the shooting of King (A1, A3), but only the Tribune's Sept. 10 dispatch says he died (A6); the other reports say he was nearly killed or taken to jail for doctors (A2, A3, A4, A8), so whether a killing occurred cannot be settled from the coverage.
Independent Tribune and Sun specials and a separate wire brief agree that a crowd stoned and beat the arrested Italian (A1, A3, A4, A6), though they disagree on whether he died.
